BUSINESS CASH PLANNING

See your cash low point before it surprises you.

Model invoice collection delay against weekly bills in under a minute — then add the payments that do not arrive every week, like the quarterly tax bill or the invoice you are still chasing. Nothing leaves this browser.

When will my business run out of cash? · vs. QuickBooks Online's Cash Flow Planner · vs. building your own spreadsheet

Money in or out on a set week

The payments that break a runway are the lumpy ones: a quarterly tax bill, an insurance renewal, a deposit you are owed. Leave a row blank if you do not need it. Fill in “Repeats every” for a bill that lands more than once in this window — a quarterly tax bill needs one row, not four.

Enter your numbers to see the forecast.

Common questions

What counts as “week 1”?

The week you are looking at the page, not a fixed calendar boundary. Each row in the results list shows both the week number and its calendar date (“w/c”), so “week 4” means something concrete when you decide which payment to move. On the defaults — $5,000 starting cash, $1,800 invoiced weekly with a 2-week collection delay, $1,400 in weekly costs — no income lands until week 3, so the lowest balance is $2,200 in week 2, before collections catch up.

Why won't it accept a collection delay like 1.5 weeks?

Because the forecast is a whole-week timeline: a fractional delay would be silently rounded up internally (1.5 forecasts identically to 2), and you would never learn the number you typed was not the number used. Rejecting it up front means the forecast always answers the delay you actually entered.

When there's a shortfall, what does the suggested fix actually do?

It targets the deepest week of the negative run, not just the first week it turns negative — covering only the first week would leave you short again days later. Then it looks for one of two moves already on your one-off list: delaying the largest outgoing payment dated at or before the shortfall starts, or pulling forward the soonest incoming payment dated after the low point. Each suggestion says plainly whether it “closes the gap” or only “covers” part of it, based on whether its amount meets the deficit at the trough. If cash recovers and then runs short again later in the window, that is a separate shortfall with its own low point, and gets its own suggestion — a payment already used to fix an earlier gap is not offered a second time.

Why does it sometimes say “this is not a timing problem”?

When your weekly costs exceed your weekly collected income — a structural gap, not a one-off — moving a single payment only postpones the same shortfall by a week rather than closing it. The planner checks for that (weekly costs minus weekly income) before suggesting a specific payment to move, so it does not sell a move-this-bill fix to a gap that reopens on its own the following week.

Why do only 3 one-off rows show at first, and why is there a limit of 8?

Three rows cover the common case — a tax bill, a renewal, a chased invoice — without cluttering the form; “Add another row” reveals more up to 8. The 8-row cap keeps the form's field set identical on every visit, which is what lets a saved draft restore correctly: the restore logic compares the saved fields against the form's fields and refuses to restore anything that doesn't match.

How do I model a bill that lands more than once, like a monthly payment?

Fill in “Repeats every” on that row with the interval in weeks — 13 for quarterly, roughly 4 for monthly — and the row lands once at the week you gave it and again every interval after that, for as long as the forecast window runs. A quarterly tax bill inside a 52-week forecast now costs one row instead of four, which matters because only 8 rows exist. Each landing still gets its own line in the results list and the CSV, and a repeating payment is still eligible to be the one a shortfall plan suggests moving — whichever occurrence actually falls inside that shortfall.

Does anything here leave my browser?

No. The forecast, the CSV export, and the saved draft all run and stay in local storage on your device. “Copy share link” puts your numbers in the URL fragment (the part after #), which a browser never sends to a server, so pasting the link somewhere else is the only way your figures travel. The only optional exception is anonymous local usage counting, which is off unless you check the box, and is disabled automatically when Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control is on.

What does “Copy share link” actually send?

It copies the current page URL with your forecast inputs — starting cash, weekly income and costs, the collection delay, the forecast length, and every filled one-off row — encoded after a # in the address. Opening that link runs the same forecast immediately, including the one-off rows, so a bookkeeper or business partner sees the exact same shortfall you did, not just the headline numbers. Anything you have not filled in is left out of the link.

Working out when one specific invoice actually pays? The invoice payment terms calculator turns terms into a due date and the day cash lands on your client's payment run — the input this forecast depends on.

Planning an HOA or condo association's multi-year capital reserve instead of a business's operating cash? The HOA reserve fund calculator projects the reserve against known component replacements and names the year a special assessment becomes likely — a different horizon than the short-term forecast here.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Cash Runway Planner

Cash Runway Planner vs. building your own cash-flow spreadsheet

A weekly running balance — starting cash, plus income offset by a collection delay, minus weekly costs, minus any one-off payments — is a formula any spreadsheet can hold. This planner does not compare against a company or a product; it compares against the sheet you would otherwise build column by column, week by week.

Where a spreadsheet and this planner produce the same number, on the calculator's own shipped defaults ($5,000 starting cash, $1,800 invoiced weekly, a 2-week collection delay, $1,400 in weekly costs, a 12-week forecast): both land on a lowest projected balance of $2,200 in week 2, before collections catch up.

Where they stop matching is the moment that balance goes negative. Add one $6,000 quarterly tax bill landing in week 4 to the same forecast, and the lowest balance drops to −$3,000 in week 4. A spreadsheet shows you that the balance is negative. This planner also names the fix: moving the $6,000 quarterly tax bill past week 11 closes the $3,000 gap, because $6,000 covers the $3,000 deficit and nothing else scheduled is closer to the shortfall. A spreadsheet does not scan its own rows for you and say that — you would have to notice the negative cell, then work out by hand which of your other rows is large enough and dated early enough to move.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What is my lowest projected balance, and when? Either tool, once built correctly — this planner's default is $2,200 in week 2.
There's a shortfall — which specific payment should I move or collect early to close it? This planner's shortfall plan, which names the payment and says whether moving it fully closes the gap or only covers part.
Is the shortfall a timing problem, or do weekly costs just exceed weekly income? This planner flags it as structural when moving one payment would only postpone the same shortfall a week later — a spreadsheet's flat balance line does not say this on its own.
I have more than eight one-off items, multiple accounts, or a forecast past 52 weeks. A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
I want to send this exact forecast to a bookkeeper or business partner. This planner's copy share link — it reopens the same figures, not a copy someone has since edited.
Run your own forecast

This tool needs no spreadsheet software, no account, and no signup: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your numbers stay on your device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this planner?

A correctly built one is — a running balance that adds weekly income (offset by your collection delay) and subtracts weekly costs and any one-off rows is ordinary arithmetic, and a spreadsheet can reproduce it column by column. The risk is not the math, it is building the formula correctly for every week, remembering to offset the income column by the collection delay, and re-doing that carefully whenever a number changes.

When is a spreadsheet actually the better choice?

When your situation has a wrinkle this planner does not model — more than eight one-off items, multiple bank accounts you want forecast separately, or a forecast horizon longer than 52 weeks. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This planner trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right structure for the common case: one account, a handful of one-off payments, and a shortfall you need a specific answer about today.

What does a blank spreadsheet not prompt you to do that this planner does?

Name the specific payment to move. A spreadsheet will show you the week the balance goes negative, but it will not, on its own, scan your other rows and tell you that delaying this $6,000 payment past this $3,000 shortfall closes the gap. It also will not tell you when the gap is not a timing problem at all — when weekly costs simply exceed weekly income — so a spreadsheet's flat balance line can make you chase a payment to move when moving one would only postpone the same shortfall a week later.

Does this replace my bookkeeping or accounting software?

No. This planner and a spreadsheet both stop at a forecast built from the starting cash, income, costs, and one-off payments you type in — neither one reads your actual bank or invoicing data, and neither is a system of record. Your bookkeeping software (or your own transaction history) is still where the real numbers you enter here come from.

Does anything here leave my browser?

No. The forecast runs and stays in local storage on your device, the same as a spreadsheet saved to your own computer. "Copy share link" puts your figures in the URL fragment, which a browser never sends to a server, so pasting that link is the only way your numbers travel — and unlike emailing a spreadsheet around, the recipient sees the exact forecast you saw, not a copy someone since edited.

vs-quickbooks-cash-flow-planner.html.text:
← Cash Runway Planner

Cash Runway Planner vs. QuickBooks Online's Cash Flow Planner

QuickBooks Online includes a Cash Flow Planner for people already running their books on the platform. Per Intuit's own help documentation, setting it up means connecting your bank and credit-card accounts so it can pull your transaction history, and it forecasts a 3-to-24-month range from that data plus any items you add by hand. It is a feature of a paid QuickBooks Online (or Intuit Enterprise Suite) subscription — it is not a standalone or free tool, and it is not available unless you are already a QuickBooks Online customer.

This calculator asks a narrower question with none of that setup: given the cash you have right now and what is coming in and out, when—if ever—does the balance go negative, and what single payment would fix it? No bank connection, no bookkeeping platform, no account. Five numbers and up to eight dated one-off rows, entirely in your browser.

QuestionWhere to answer it
My books already live in QuickBooks Online with bank feeds connected — what does my cash balance look like 3–24 months out? QuickBooks Online's Cash Flow Planner.
I don't use QuickBooks (or don't want to connect my bank) — when does my cash go negative over the next 12 months? This calculator's weekly forecast — no account, no bank connection.
There's a projected shortfall — which specific payment should I move or collect early to close it? This calculator's shortfall plan, which names the payment and says whether it fully closes the gap.
Is the shortfall a timing problem, or do weekly costs just exceed weekly income? This calculator names it as structural when moving one payment would only postpone the same shortfall.
I need a one-time item like a tax bill or an insurance renewal on a specific date. Both tools support this — QuickBooks calls it an "event"; this calculator calls it a one-off row.
Run your own forecast

This tool needs no QuickBooks account, no bank connection, and no signup: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your numbers stay on your device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or QuickBooks Online's Cash Flow Planner?

It depends on what you already have. QuickBooks Online's Cash Flow Planner is a feature inside a paid QuickBooks Online (or Intuit Enterprise Suite) subscription: setting it up means connecting your bank and credit-card accounts so it can read your transaction history, and it is only available if you are already a QuickBooks Online customer. This calculator is a free standalone page: no account, no subscription, and no bank connection. You type your starting cash, weekly income, weekly costs, and any one-off payments directly, and the forecast runs in your browser. If your books already live in QuickBooks Online and your accounts are connected, its planner can lean on that transaction history. If you are not a QuickBooks customer, or just want a fast answer before committing numbers to any accounting software, this page answers the same question with five fields and no signup.

Can QuickBooks' Cash Flow Planner handle a one-off payment like a tax bill?

Yes, and so can this calculator — both let you add a dated one-time item separate from your recurring income and costs. QuickBooks' planner calls this an "event": you name it, give it an amount, mark it money in or money out, and pick the date. This calculator's one-off rows work the same way, up to eight of them. The difference is what happens after you enter one: this calculator also names which specific one-off payment to move (or which invoice to collect early) to close a projected shortfall, and separately flags when the gap is not a timing problem at all — when weekly costs simply exceed weekly income — so moving a payment would only postpone the same shortfall rather than fix it.

What forecast range does each tool cover?

QuickBooks Online's Cash Flow Planner supports a forecast range from 3 months out to 24 months, per Intuit's own help documentation. This calculator forecasts up to 52 weeks (about 12 months), with every week shown against its actual calendar date. Neither is strictly longer than the other across their full range — pick QuickBooks' planner for a multi-year view once you are on the platform, or this page for a shorter, week-by-week runway check with no setup.

Is this page affiliated with Intuit or QuickBooks?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Intuit Inc. QuickBooks, QuickBooks Online, and Cash Flow Planner are trademarks of Intuit Inc., named here only to describe what this calculator is for.

when-will-i-run-out-of-cash.html.text:
← Cash runway planner

When will my business run out of cash?

Profit and cash are not the same question. A business that is profitable on paper can still run out of cash the week a quarterly tax bill or an insurance renewal lands on top of the usual bills, because invoices arrive later than the costs they are meant to cover. The date that matters is not the lowest week in a forecast — it is the first week the running balance goes negative, because that is the date an invoice or a bill has to move in front of.

Open the free cash runway planner

What a weekly average cannot see

Payments that do not repeat. A forecast built only from a smoothed weekly average answers "cash stays positive" to an owner who is about to be $3,000 down the week the quarterly tax bill clears — which is worse than no answer, because they believe it.

The first negative week versus the lowest week. Covering only the deepest week's shortfall can still leave a business short earlier in the run; the first negative week is the date to act, the deepest week is how much to move.

Structural gaps disguised as timing problems. If weekly costs already exceed weekly collections before any one-off payment is counted, moving one payment around only postpones the same shortfall — it does not fix it.

A number you can defend

  1. Enter starting cash, weekly income invoiced, the collection delay in whole weeks, and weekly costs.
  2. Add each payment that does not repeat as its own dated row: a description, an amount, the week it lands, and whether it is money in or money out.
  3. Set the forecast length — long enough to include the next quarterly bill, up to 52 weeks.
  4. Read the first projected shortfall week, not just the lowest balance, and check which dated payment the planner names as able to close the gap.

Worked example

Starting cash, weekly income with a two-week collection delay, and weekly costs project a first shortfall in week 2, $3,000.00 short at the low point. A Quarterly tax payment of $6,000.00 is scheduled in week 2; moving it past week 5 closes the gap entirely. Alternatively, an Invoice 118 for $4,000.00 due in week 6 would close the gap if collected before week 2. The planner reports both options and states plainly when neither can help — because weekly costs already exceed weekly income, which is a structural gap no scheduling change fixes.

Common questions

How do I calculate when my business will run out of cash?

Forecast weekly balance from starting cash, weekly invoiced income delayed by your collection lag, and weekly costs, then schedule the payments that do not repeat — a quarterly tax bill, an insurance renewal, a deposit you are owed — in the exact week each lands. The answer is the first week the running balance goes negative, not a smoothed average.

Should I fix the lowest week or the first negative week?

Both, for different reasons. How much to move is sized off the deepest week in the negative run, because covering only the first week's gap leaves you short again days later. When to act is the first negative week, because that is the date the fix has to already be in place — by the trough it is too late to move anything dated earlier.

Which payment should I move to close a cash gap?

Delaying only helps an outflow dated at or before the shortfall starts, so the planner looks there and picks the largest one. Pulling money forward only helps an inflow dated after the trough, so it picks the earliest one large enough to matter. If weekly costs already exceed weekly income before any one-off is counted, moving a payment only postpones the shortfall — the planner calls that out as a structural gap, not a timing problem.
